name: Infosys
summary: Infosys hires most freshers in India through campus and off-campus drives that start with an online test of aptitude, reasoning, verbal ability and pseudocode or coding, followed by technical and HR interviews that candidates often describe as short and resume-based. It also runs HackWithInfy, a coding competition for engineering students that can lead to pre-placement interviews, and it describes its values as C-LIFE.
rounds: Online test (aptitude, reasoning, verbal, pseudocode or coding)

covers: Education, your strongest skill and one project, in about a minute
What you did yourself in that project, with one result
Why this role is the next step for you

questions.text: Which programming language are you most comfortable in, and why?
covers: One language and what you've actually built with it
A feature you like and a limitation you've run into
How you'd pick up a different language if a project needed it

questions.text: Explain normalization in databases with an example.
covers: Why normalise: less repeated data and fewer update, insert and delete problems
1NF, 2NF and 3NF in a line each, shown on a small table such as students and courses
When a team might denormalise on purpose, for example to speed up reports
Specific reasons: its training for new joiners, the range of clients, a service line you're interested in
A link between those reasons and your own skills or goals
Something recent you've read about its work, not just its size

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in five years?
covers: A realistic direction: deeper in a technology, or towards design or leading a small team
The skills you plan to build to get there
How growing inside the company fits that plan

questions.text: Tell me about a time you took the lead in a group project without being asked.
covers: What was stuck or missing and why you stepped in
How you got others on board without a title, for example by doing the hard part first
The outcome for the project and what the team said

questions.text: Tell me about a time you admitted a mistake even though it made you look bad.
covers: The mistake, owned plainly in the first person
Who you told, how quickly, and what you offered to fix
What you do differently now

questions.text: Tell me about a time you went beyond the brief because it helped the people who would use your work.
covers: Who the users were and what they actually needed
What extra you did and why it was worth the time
How you know it helped them

questions.text: Tell me about a time work in a team wasn't shared fairly. What did you do?
covers: What was uneven, described without blaming anyone
How you raised it or rebalanced the work
The result for the team and the deadline

questions.text: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
covers: A process has its own memory; threads inside a process share it
Why threads are cheaper to create but need care with shared data
An everyday example, such as a browser with tabs or a music player

questions.text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL? Give an example.
covers: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY
An example such as departments with more than five employees
Why aggregate functions belong in HAVING, not WHERE

questions.text: How would you design the database for a simple library management system?
covers: Main tables: books, members, loans, maybe authors, with their keys
How a loan links a member and a book, and how returns and fines are recorded
One or two queries it must answer, such as overdue books

questions.text: For experienced candidates: how did your team handle a change in client requirements halfway through a release?
covers: What changed and why the client needed it
How the team assessed the impact on scope, effort and dates
What was agreed with the client and how it was delivered

questions.text: Are you open to working on any technology the project needs, even if it isn't your first choice?
covers: An honest yes, with a preference you can state politely
An example of learning something you didn't choose and doing it well
How you'd keep building your preferred skills alongside

tips: Keep 'tell me about yourself' to a minute: education, project, skills, why this role.
Expect questions on whatever you wrote on your resume, so only list what you can explain.
Practise reading short pseudocode and predicting its output; the online test often includes it.
Go deep in one language rather than thin in several: the technical round often stays with the language you name.
Prepare a short story for a few of the C-LIFE values, such as leading by example or being transparent about a mistake.
If you've taken part in HackWithInfy, be ready to explain how you approached its problems.
